correctness.rationale: The five structural conditions are necessary: vertex-cover feasibility forces at least one center and forces all leaves incident to an omitted center, while two omitted leaves adjacent to one center make the corresponding pendant edges edge-metrically indistinguishable. They are sufficient because selected leaves separate same-side pendant edges, a selected center separates opposite-side pendant edges, and either the opposite center or a forced opposite leaf separates the central edge from a pendant edge. The three disjoint center-selection cases expand exactly to the stated polynomial. The independent exhaustive checker agrees for all parameter pairs from one through five.

evidence: Theorem 2.4 proves that a graph with \(m\) pendant vertices has dominant edge metric dimension at least \(m\).
Example 3.3 specializes this to the uniform caterpillar \(T_{l,t}=P_l\circ\overline{K_t}\), giving \(\operatorname{Ddim}_e(T_{l,t})=lt\).
Taking \(l=2\) covers the scalar value for the balanced double star \(S_{t,t}\), but neither theorem enumerates generators or handles unequal leaf multiplicities through an all-set statement.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The strongest prior family result was treated as real coverage rather than ignored. It subsumes one scalar subfamily, so the accepted claim is framed around the all-generator characterization and polynomial; these require new edge-pair and vertex-cover arguments.

originality.rationale: The primary introducing paper gives a pendant lower bound and a corona formula. Its uniform-caterpillar example already implies the balanced double-star scalar value, so the accepted novelty is deliberately narrower and stronger in a different direction: arbitrary unequal double stars, every dominant edge metric generator, the complete cardinality enumerator, and the exact count of bases. No inspected or searched source supplied that classification.
residual_risks: The balanced scalar subfamily is prior-covered and is not claimed as original.

value.rationale: Double stars are the canonical diameter-three trees with exactly two branching centers and the first nonuniform extension of the published uniform caterpillar example. The full feasible-set classification turns the target invariant from a single optimum value into an exact structural profile, handles arbitrary imbalance, and gives the basis multiplicity and every possible generator size. This is a natural complete classification rather than an arbitrary finite slice.
